clue.text: My home has identity taken over by mere relation

indicators.note: when a post is taken over by someone new, the old holder is ousted and the newcomer sits in the same place

blocks.note: cor! is an exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
a residence is where one lives
ID is the usual short form of identity
a mere is a small lake, so a pond

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that their house now carries the name of a minor relative.
explanation.walkthrough: COR + RESIDENCE with its ID swapped for POND gives CORRESPONDENCE. 'Mere' looks like 'only', but here it is the noun for a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A correspondence between two things is a matching link or analogy between them, which is a kind of relation.

clue.text: Charlie upset misspelling, penning account that’s duplicated

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in, as in a pen for sheep
in a down entry, to upset is to tip over so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Charlie is the NATO alphabet word for C
a typo is a printing or typing error
AC is a standard abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: An accountant spots a spelling slip in a copied entry and gets annoyed about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The account goes inside the misspelling just after its first letter, and the whole run is then turned upside down beneath Charlie. 'Upset' looks like annoyed, matching the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Copycat is used as an adjective for something imitating an original, as in a copycat crime, so it describes what is duplicated.

clue.text: Over river, remedied a poorly run upcoming music venue

indicators.note: something remedied has been put right, so these letters are fixed into a new order
in a down entry, coming up means reading from the bottom towards the top
in a down entry, one part placed over another sits above it in the column

blocks.note: letters taken as printed, to be rearranged
to hare is to run fast
the Ouse is one of several English rivers with that name

explanation.surface: A badly managed music club by a river has been put right ahead of its reopening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poorly run' reads as one phrase about management, but 'poorly' is anagram fodder and 'run' is a separate word, read upwards. The Ouse is a river in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Opera House in Covent Garden, London, is the home of the Royal Opera and Royal Ballet, a famous place to hear music.

clue.text: Both stripped, wet Welsh swimmers

indicators.note: stripping a word takes off its outer layer, its first and last letters, and 'both' applies that to the two words that follow

blocks.note: the inside of the word once its ends are removed
the inside of the word once its ends are removed

explanation.surface: Two naked, soaking Welsh bathers have just been for a swim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both' tells you the stripping applies to each of the next two words, not to the word 'Both' itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are long fish that live and move in water, so they are a fair example of swimmers.

clue.text: Plant for all to see in sheds

indicators.note: to shed something is to cast it off, as a tree drops leaves

blocks.note: something in is fashionable, liked by many
U is the British film rating meaning suitable for all audiences

explanation.surface: Garden sheds are put on public display, with plants inside them.
explanation.walkthrough: POPULAR loses its U. 'Sheds' looks like a noun for garden huts, but it is a verb meaning casts off. U is the British film certificate for universal viewing.
explanation.definitionFit: A poplar is a tall, fast-growing tree, and any tree is a plant in the botanical sense.

clue.text: Sailor’s uniform covered by awkwardly lain cat

indicators.note: something placed awkwardly is set down clumsily and out of order
what is covered is wrapped round by something else on the outside

blocks.note: Uniform is the NATO alphabet word for U
letters taken as printed, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor's uniform is draped over by a cat lying in an uncomfortable position.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'uniform' in the surface is clothing; in the wordplay it is just the letter U, from the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Nautical means relating to sailors, ships or navigation, so it can stand for the possessive 'sailor's' as in nautical terms.

clue.text: Catch me up on motorway cutting through county ridge

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top
something cutting through another passes into its middle, ending up inside it
in a down entry, one part on another sits on top of it in the column

blocks.note: to nab is to catch
taken as printed
Kent is a county in south-east England
M is the prefix of British motorway names, like the M25

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a lift on the motorway where it slices through a ridge in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch me up' reads as a request to wait for someone; it is two words read upwards. Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: An embankment is a raised bank of earth built to carry a road or hold back water, so a man-made ridge.

clue.text: Airline using carbon in routes supporting token offsets

indicators.note: one thing in another is held inside it
in a down entry, a part supporting another sits underneath it in the column

blocks.note: a counter is a token used in games
BA is British Airways
shipping and flight paths are called lanes
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: An airline pays for token carbon offsets to excuse the emissions on its routes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carbon offsets' looks like one environmental phrase, but 'offsets' is the definition and 'carbon' only gives C. BA is the code for British Airways.
explanation.definitionFit: To counterbalance something is to weigh against it and cancel its effect, which is what offsetting does.

clue.text: Trembles removing head and organs of animal

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is taken off here

blocks.note: something that judders shakes violently

explanation.surface: A beheaded animal's body still shakes while its organs are taken out by a butcher.
explanation.walkthrough: JUDDERS without its J. SHUDDERS would also tremble, but losing one letter leaves HUDDERS, so it is the wrong verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An udder is the milk-producing gland of a cow, goat or sheep, a bodily organ of those animals.

clue.text: Notice of employee’s return for work?

definitions.text: Notice of employee’s return for work?

blocks.note: surface reading: a notice that a worker is coming back after time off
setter's reading: the return is the earnings a worker gets for their labour, and the notice is the slip that itemises them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' tempts you to think of someone coming back to the office; it means what the job pays back, and the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A pay slip is the statement given to an employee showing wages earned and deductions, a written notice of earnings.

clue.text: Article in French with heading that’s clear

blocks.note: un is the French for 'a', an indefinite article
heading somewhere is being bound for it

explanation.surface: A French newspaper piece carries a headline that is easy to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading' looks like a headline, but it is the sense 'on the way to', as in bound for home.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unbound is free of ties or restraints, and clear can mean free of obstruction or entanglement.

clue.text: Bitter cop leaving work early

indicators.note: when one thing is leaving another it departs, so those letters go away

blocks.note: taken as printed
op is short for opus, a musical work
early can mean ancient, belonging to an old period, as in early man

explanation.surface: A resentful police officer slips off from his shift before time is up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving work early' reads as one phrase about clocking off; split it, so 'leaving work' acts on the cop and 'early' is a separate word, in its sense of ancient.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter weather is piercingly chilly, as in a bitter wind, so the adjective is a synonym in that sense.

clue.text: Doll from Orient manufactured in China

indicators.note: to manufacture is to make something up from raw material, so these letters are reworked
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: china is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, from 'china plate'
letters taken as printed, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A doll imported from the Far East turns out to be made in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' in the surface is the country, but in Cockney rhyming slang china (plate) means mate, a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A marionette is a puppet worked by strings, a jointed figure that is a kind of doll.

clue.text: Trading from car upon turning 18

indicators.note: turning things over mixes them about, so the letters come out in a new order
in a down entry, one part upon another sits on top of it in the column

blocks.note: a Merc is a Mercedes car
the answer to 18 Across

explanation.surface: Someone earns a living selling cars once they reach eighteen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning 18' reads as reaching that age; 18 is a cross-reference to the answer at 18 Across, whose letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercantile means relating to merchants and commerce, so it fits trading used as an adjective, as in a trading nation.

clue.text: Reached summit of fell overlooking loch

indicators.note: to overlook something is to miss it out, so it is left out of the word

blocks.note: toppled means fell over
L is a map abbreviation for loch or lake

explanation.surface: A walker climbs to the top of a northern hill with a view down over a Scottish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like a hill, which the surface needs, but here it is the past tense of fall. Overlooking also has its sense of having a view over.
explanation.definitionFit: To top a hill is to get to its highest point, so topped means reached its summit.

clue.text: With affirmation, political theorist reportedly signs for course

indicators.note: what is reportedly so is passed on by word of mouth, so judged by sound

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with
ay is an old or dialect form of yes
Karl Marx was the German political theorist behind communism

explanation.surface: A famous political thinker signs up for a course of study, agreeing to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests lessons, which goes with the theorist, but it is the route of a walk. Note the homophone covers only the theorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Waymarks are posts or symbols set along a footpath to show walkers which way to go, signs for following a route.

clue.text: Monsters head over close to other snakelike characters

indicators.note: turning something over flips it round so it reads the other way
the close of a word is its end, so its final letter is kept

blocks.note: to head somewhere is to go there
the last letter of the word
the letter S is shaped like a snake, and its name is spelt ess

explanation.surface: Monsters slither towards one another, the leader moving closer with serpentine figures behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' here are letters of the alphabet: an S curves like a snake, and its name is written ESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogresses are female ogres, man-eating giants of folklore, so they are monsters.

clue.text: Way to enter pen, mature pet’s container

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it

blocks.note: a Bic is a familiar make of ballpoint pen
RD is the abbreviation for road
to age is to mature or grow older

explanation.surface: Directions for getting an older pet into its enclosure or carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' seems to belong with the pet as an animal enclosure; it is a writing pen, a BIC. 'Mature' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A birdcage holds a pet bird such as a budgie or canary, so it is a container for a pet.

clue.text: Mark overheard plots

indicators.note: something overheard is caught by ear, so the clue works on sound

blocks.note: trouble brews when someone plots or schemes it

explanation.surface: Mark is caught eavesdropping on schemes, a man named Mark overhearing conspiracies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name, but it is a mark on the skin, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bruise is a discoloured patch on the skin caused by a blow, a mark left on the body.

clue.text: Involve row hiding at back

indicators.note: something hiding another keeps it tucked away inside
going back means running the other way, from right to left

blocks.note: a line is a row of people or things
taken as printed

explanation.surface: A quarrel is being kept hidden behind the scenes and involves several people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' tempts as a quarrel, matching the surface, but it is a line. AT goes into LINE and the result is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail something is to bring it in as a necessary part or consequence, which is what involving it means.

clue.text: Bottom of pool bishop splits leaked fluid

indicators.note: something fluid flows and has no fixed form, so the letters can take another shape
what splits something forces its way into the middle of it

blocks.note: letters taken as printed, to be rearranged
B is the chess notation for a bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop's swim ends badly when the pool cracks and the water leaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fluid' looks like the noun for the leaked liquid, but it is an adjective telling you to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lakebed is the ground under a lake, and a lake is a large pool, so it is a pool's bottom.

clue.text: Soldiers almost trap founder of tribe

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the RE are the Royal Engineers of the British Army
a U-bend is the trap in a drainpipe that holds water to block smells

explanation.surface: A band of soldiers nearly manages to ambush the leader of a tribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' looks like a verb for capture; it is the plumbing noun, the curved pipe under a sink.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, Reuben was Jacob's eldest son, and the tribe of Reuben, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, descends from him.

clue.text: Endured running around hours before reaching home straight

indicators.note: what comes before reaching something is placed just ahead of it
something running moves about freely, so the letters are set loose into a new order
to go around something is to enclose it on both sides

blocks.note: letters taken as printed, to be rearranged
H is the abbreviation for hours
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A runner kept going for hours before reaching the home straight of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home straight' reads as one racing phrase, but it splits: 'home' gives IN, 'straight' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Straight can mean direct and free of obstacles, as in a straight run, which is what unhindered progress is.

clue.text: Way king rules after reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things the other way round

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
law is a body of rules

explanation.surface: A monarch decides policy only after careful thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflection' reads as careful thought, but it is a mirror image. 'Rules' is a noun, not the king's verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A walk is a path or route laid out for walking, as in a riverside walk, so it is a way.

clue.text: Elevated foursome involved in collaborative dance

indicators.note: what is involved in something is wrapped up inside it
in a down entry, raised letters read upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.note: four letters running inside the word
tells you the length of the run

explanation.surface: Two couples lift each other high in a dance done together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foursome' sounds like dancers, but it just tells you the length of the run of letters to take.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is a formal social gathering for dancing, so the word names a kind of dance.

clue.text: Examines nail that is beginning to split

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a stud is a large-headed nail
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone inspects a fingernail that is starting to crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nail' suggests a fingernail cracking; it is a stud, the heavy nail in a door.
explanation.definitionFit: To study something is to look at it closely and carefully, which is what examining it means.

clue.text: Shaggy-haired youth having hump with group, getting left out

indicators.note: something out is no longer there, so that letter goes

blocks.note: to hump a load is to carry or bear it
a club is a group of members
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A long-haired teenager in a grump joins a gang, only to be excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having the hump' is British for being in a sulk, which the surface uses; here hump is a verb meaning carry.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear cub is a young bear, covered in thick fur, so the clue describes it whimsically as a shaggy youngster.

clue.text: Unemotional act involving a fighter splitting up lads

indicators.note: what involves something takes it in, enclosing it
something splitting another breaks into it and ends up in the middle

blocks.note: a deed is an act
a means per, as in ten pounds a head
sons are boys, lads
Muhammad Ali, the boxer

explanation.surface: A boxer breaks up a gang of lads in a cold, businesslike manner.
explanation.walkthrough: The small word 'a' is easy to skip, but it gives PER, as in ten pence a mile. The fighter is the boxer Muhammad Ali.
explanation.definitionFit: Depersonalised means stripped of individual feeling or character, impersonal, so it describes something unemotional.
